title: Bone tumours: age, site, X-ray sign & genetics
subject: Orthopedics
anchor: Teen + distal femur metaphysis + sunburst/Codman triangle → osteosarcoma; child + diaphysis + onion peel + fever/↑ESR → Ewing sarcoma.
Skeletally mature 20–40 y + eccentric epiphyseal lytic 'soap bubble' reaching subchondral bone → giant cell tumour.
Night pain relieved by aspirin/NSAID + small radiolucent nidus with dense sclerosis → osteoid osteoma.
Central metaphyseal cyst proximal humerus + 'fallen fragment' → unicameral bone cyst; eccentric expansile 'blow-out' with fluid–fluid levels → ABC.
algorithm:
Bone lesion on X-ray
→ Note age, site along bone (epiphysis / metaphysis / diaphysis), margins, matrix, periosteal reaction
  Aggressive (wide zone of transition, permeative, sunburst/Codman/onion peel) → MRI whole bone (skip lesions) + CT chest + bone scan → biopsy LAST, along planned incision line, at the treating centre
  Benign-looking & asymptomatic (osteochondroma, NOF) → observe
→ Stage (Enneking) → treat:
  Osteosarcoma → neoadjuvant chemo (MAP: methotrexate, doxorubicin, cisplatin) → limb salvage wide resection → adjuvant chemo
  Ewing → chemo + surgery and/or radiotherapy (radiosensitive)
  GCT → extended curettage + adjuvant (phenol/cement) ± denosumab
  Chondrosarcoma → wide excision (chemo- & radio-resistant)
  Osteoid osteoma → NSAIDs or CT-guided radiofrequency ablation
Pathological fracture risk in metastasis → Mirels' score: ≥9 prophylactic fixation, 8 borderline, ≤7 radiotherapy/observe

head: Points
Site
Pain
Lesion

points: **Most common primary malignant bone tumour** (excluding myeloma) = osteosarcoma; most common malignant bone tumour overall = metastasis; most common primary malignant overall incl. haematological = multiple myeloma.
**Most common benign bone tumour** = osteochondroma; malignant change in a solitary lesion is rare (<1%), higher in hereditary multiple exostoses.
Ewing sarcoma mimics osteomyelitis: fever, leucocytosis, ↑ESR — biopsy differentiates.
GCT is the classic epiphyseal tumour of the skeletally MATURE; chondroblastoma is the epiphyseal tumour of the skeletally IMMATURE.
**Enneking staging**: benign 1 latent / 2 active / 3 aggressive; malignant I low grade, II high grade, III metastasis; A intracompartmental, B extracompartmental.
**Mirels' score** (4 items, each 1–3, total 4–12): ≥9 → prophylactic internal fixation; 8 → clinical judgement; ≤7 → radiotherapy and observe.
Biopsy is the last step of work-up and should be done by the surgeon who will resect, with the track excised en bloc at definitive surgery.
Lytic metastases: kidney, thyroid, lung; blastic: prostate, breast (mixed), carcinoid; most common site of skeletal metastasis = spine (vertebral body; pedicle 'winking owl' sign).
Osteosarcoma variants: parosteal (posterior distal femur, low grade, best prognosis), telangiectatic (lytic, mimics ABC), secondary (Paget's, post-radiation).

traps.stem: A 14-year-old with a painful lytic epiphyseal lesion of the proximal humerus with sclerotic rim and stippled calcification; physis is open.
traps.trap: Giant cell tumour — because it is the 'epiphyseal tumour'.
traps.fix: Chondroblastoma. GCT occurs after physeal closure (20–40 y); epiphyseal lesion with an open physis = chondroblastoma.

traps.stem: Young man with nocturnal tibial pain dramatically relieved by aspirin; X-ray shows cortical sclerosis with a tiny lucency.
traps.trap: Brodie abscess or stress fracture — both cause cortical sclerosis.
traps.fix: Osteoid osteoma (nidus on CT is diagnostic); PGE₂ production explains NSAID response; treat with CT-guided radiofrequency ablation.

traps.stem: Metastatic breast cancer: lytic lesion in the subtrochanteric femur involving >2/3 cortex with pain on walking.
traps.trap: Radiotherapy alone, since metastases are radiosensitive.
traps.fix: Mirels' = 3 (peritrochanteric) + 3 (functional pain) + 3 (lytic) + 3 (>2/3) = 12 → prophylactic fixation first (then radiotherapy).

cards.back: Giant cell tumour of bone; denosumab (anti-RANKL).

cards.text: The 'fallen fragment' sign is characteristic of a {{c1::unicameral (simple) bone cyst}}, most often in the {{c2::proximal humerus}}.

cards.front: Mirels' score threshold for prophylactic fixation?
cards.back: ≥9 (8 = borderline, ≤7 = radiotherapy/observe).

cards.front: Osteoid osteoma vs osteoblastoma — size and NSAID response?
cards.back: Osteoid osteoma: nidus <1.5–2 cm, pain relieved by NSAIDs. Osteoblastoma: >2 cm, spine posterior elements, pain not relieved by NSAIDs.

cards.text: Osteosarcoma: classic site {{c1::distal femur metaphysis}}; radiographic signs {{c2::sunburst}} and {{c3::Codman triangle}}; commonest site of metastasis {{c4::lung}}.

title: Upper limb fractures & shoulder dislocation
subject: Orthopedics
anchor: Child, FOOSH, swollen elbow with S-shaped deformity, absent radial pulse → extension supracondylar fracture; watch for Volkmann ischaemia (pain on passive finger extension).
Elderly woman, FOOSH, 'dinner fork' → Colles (dorsal tilt); 'garden spade' → Smith (volar); intra-articular rim + carpal subluxation → Barton.
Snuffbox tenderness with normal X-ray → treat as scaphoid fracture (proximal pole AVN).
Arm held abducted & externally rotated, flattened deltoid, regimental-badge numbness → anterior shoulder dislocation with axillary nerve injury.
algorithm:
Supracondylar humerus fracture (child)
→ Check radial pulse, capillary refill, AIN (OK sign), radial, ulnar nerve
→ Gartland I (undisplaced) → above-elbow cast ~3 wk
→ Gartland II (posterior cortex intact, hinged) → closed reduction ± percutaneous K-wires (CRPP)
→ Gartland III (completely displaced) → urgent CRPP; open reduction if irreducible/vascular injury
  Pink pulseless hand after reduction → close observation; white pulseless → explore brachial artery
  Pain on passive finger stretch, pain out of proportion → compartment syndrome → fasciotomy
Scaphoid suspected (snuffbox/scaphoid tubercle tenderness)
→ X-ray scaphoid views → if negative: immobilise + repeat X-ray at 10–14 days, or MRI (best early test)
→ Undisplaced waist → cast (or percutaneous screw); displaced/proximal pole → ORIF (Herbert screw)

head: Type
Injury
Management
rows: AC torn, CC intact; slight elevation

points: Supracondylar fracture: **extension type ~95%**; most commonly injured nerve overall = **anterior interosseous nerve** (loss of OK sign); posteromedial displacement → radial nerve; flexion type → ulnar nerve; medial K-wire → iatrogenic ulnar nerve.
Most common complication of supracondylar fracture = **malunion → cubitus varus (gunstock)**; it is cosmetic, carrying angle lost.
**Volkmann ischaemic contracture**: brachial artery injury → forearm flexor (FDP, FPL) ischaemia; earliest sign is pain on passive finger extension; pulse may still be present.
**Scaphoid**: commonest carpal fracture, waist commonest site; retrograde blood supply (dorsal branch of radial artery enters distally) → proximal pole AVN and non-union.
**Neer classification** of proximal humerus: 4 parts (head, shaft, greater and lesser tuberosity); a part is 'displaced' if >1 cm or >45° angulation.
**Shoulder dislocation**: anterior (subcoracoid) >95%; Bankart lesion = anteroinferior labral tear; Hill-Sachs = posterolateral humeral head impaction; recurrent dislocation commonest in young.
**Posterior dislocation**: epileptic seizure or electric shock; arm locked in internal rotation; 'light bulb' sign on AP; reverse Hill-Sachs (McLaughlin) lesion; easily missed — get axillary view.
Tests for anterior dislocation: Duga's test (cannot touch opposite shoulder), Hamilton ruler test, Callaway (↑ axillary girth); reduction — Kocher, Hippocratic, Stimson, external rotation.
Fracture surgical neck humerus and anterior dislocation → **axillary nerve**; shaft (spiral groove) → radial nerve; medial epicondyle → ulnar nerve.

traps.stem: 7-year-old with displaced extension supracondylar fracture cannot flex the IP joint of the thumb and DIP of the index finger; sensation intact.
traps.trap: Median nerve injury — but sensation would be lost.
traps.fix: Anterior interosseous nerve (pure motor branch of median) — the commonest nerve injured in extension-type supracondylar fracture.

traps.stem: Fall on outstretched hand; anatomical snuffbox tender; wrist X-ray normal.
traps.trap: Discharge as wrist sprain because X-ray is normal.
traps.fix: Immobilise in a scaphoid/thumb spica cast and repeat X-ray at 10–14 days or get MRI; missed scaphoid fracture → non-union/AVN of proximal pole.

traps.stem: Man after a seizure has a painful shoulder held in internal rotation; AP X-ray 'looks normal'.
traps.fix: Posterior shoulder dislocation — light bulb sign; confirm with axillary/scapular Y view.

cards.text: Gartland II supracondylar fracture = displaced with {{c1::intact posterior cortex}}; Gartland III = {{c2::completely displaced}} — treated by {{c3::closed reduction and percutaneous pinning}}.

cards.front: Monteggia vs Galeazzi — which bone fractures and what dislocates?
cards.back: Monteggia: proximal ulna fracture + radial head dislocation (PIN at risk). Galeazzi: distal radius shaft fracture + DRUJ dislocation.

cards.text: Hill-Sachs lesion is impaction of the {{c1::posterolateral humeral head}}; Bankart lesion is a tear of the {{c2::anteroinferior glenoid labrum}}.

cards.front: Why does the proximal pole of the scaphoid undergo AVN?
cards.back: Retrograde blood supply: branches of the radial artery enter the distal pole/waist dorsally, so a waist fracture devascularises the proximal pole.

cards.front: Earliest and most reliable sign of impending Volkmann ischaemia after a supracondylar fracture?
cards.back: Pain on passive extension of the fingers (pain out of proportion); pulselessness is late/unreliable.

cards.text: Rockwood AC injury: type {{c1::III}} = AC and CC ligaments torn with 25–100% displacement; types {{c2::IV–VI}} need surgery.

title: Lower limb fractures, open fractures, physeal injuries & compartment syndrome
subject: Orthopedics
anchor: Elderly woman, trivial fall, shortened slightly externally rotated leg → intracapsular neck of femur (AVN, non-union); marked external rotation + more shortening → intertrochanteric.
Dashboard injury, limb flexed–adducted–internally rotated, foot drop → posterior hip dislocation with sciatic (peroneal division) nerve injury.
Pain out of proportion + pain on passive stretch after tibial fracture → compartment syndrome → fasciotomy.
algorithm:
Neck of femur fracture
→ Age <60–65 / physiologically young → urgent anatomical reduction + internal fixation (cancellous screws / DHS) regardless of Garden type
→ Elderly:
  Garden I–II (undisplaced) → internal fixation
  Garden III–IV (displaced) → hemiarthroplasty; total hip replacement if active/independent or pre-existing arthritis
Intertrochanteric → stable: DHS; unstable/reverse oblique/subtrochanteric extension → proximal femoral nail
Open fracture
→ IV antibiotics as early as possible (ideally within 1 h) + tetanus prophylaxis + photo, saline-soaked dressing, splint
→ Formal debridement in theatre; classify Gustilo-Anderson AFTER debridement
→ Skeletal stabilisation; soft-tissue cover (ideally within 72 h–7 days for III B)
Compartment syndrome
→ Clinical diagnosis; if equivocal measure pressure: ΔP (diastolic − compartment) <30 mmHg (or absolute >30 mmHg) → fasciotomy (leg: 2 incisions, 4 compartments)

Grades

A below (stable) · B at level · C above (syndesmosis torn — unstable, needs fixation); Lauge-Hansen: supination–external rotation commonest

points: Main blood supply to the adult femoral head = **medial circumflex femoral artery** (retinacular branches) → displaced intracapsular fractures risk AVN and non-union; intertrochanteric (extracapsular) rarely gets AVN but malunites into coxa vara.
**Posterior hip dislocation** (commonest, ~90%): flexion, adduction, internal rotation, shortening; sciatic nerve (peroneal division) injury; reduce urgently (ideally <6 h) to reduce AVN.
**Anterior hip dislocation**: flexion, abduction, external rotation; femoral/obturator neurovascular structures at risk.
**Hawkins sign**: subchondral lucency of the talar dome at 6–8 weeks = revascularisation → AVN unlikely.
**Gustilo antibiotics**: I/II → first-generation cephalosporin (cefazolin); III → add Gram-negative cover (gentamicin); farmyard/soil contamination → add high-dose penicillin (Clostridium).
**Maisonneuve fracture**: proximal fibula fracture + medial malleolus/deltoid injury with syndesmotic disruption — always X-ray the whole leg in medial ankle injury.

**Compartment syndrome**: earliest symptom = pain out of proportion; earliest sign = pain on passive stretch; pulselessness is a LATE sign; commonest cause = tibial shaft fracture; commonest compartment = anterior of leg.
Salter-Harris mnemonic SALTR: Straight, Above, Lower, Through, Rammed (crush). V has worst growth prognosis.
Clinical: NOF fracture → slight external rotation, can't SLR; intertrochanteric → marked external rotation (>45°, lateral border of foot on bed), more shortening, more bruising.

traps.stem: 42-year-old manual labourer, Garden IV fracture neck of femur after a road accident.
traps.trap: Hemiarthroplasty, because Garden III–IV is treated by replacement.
traps.fix: Young patient → urgent anatomical reduction + internal fixation to save the head; arthroplasty is for the elderly.

traps.stem: Tibial fracture in plaster; severe pain, dorsalis pedis pulse palpable.
traps.trap: Compartment syndrome excluded because the pulse is present.
traps.fix: Compartment pressure exceeds capillary perfusion long before arterial occlusion; pulses persist — split cast and do fasciotomy if pain on passive stretch.

traps.stem: Open tibial fracture with 3 cm wound, extensive periosteal stripping requiring a flap, no vascular injury.
traps.fix: Gustilo IIIB: grade by soft-tissue damage/energy (and need for flap), not wound length alone.

cards.text: Posterior hip dislocation: limb in {{c1::flexion, adduction and internal rotation}}; nerve at risk {{c2::sciatic (peroneal division)}}.

cards.front: Gustilo IIIB vs IIIC?
cards.back: IIIB: extensive soft-tissue loss with periosteal stripping needing flap cover. IIIC: arterial injury requiring repair.

cards.text: Commonest Salter-Harris type is {{c1::II}}; the type with the worst prognosis for growth is {{c2::V (crush)}}.

cards.front: Pauwels type III femoral neck fracture — why does it matter?
cards.back: Fracture line >50° from horizontal → vertical shear forces → highest risk of non-union and fixation failure.

cards.text: Fasciotomy is indicated when ΔP (diastolic BP − compartment pressure) is {{c1::<30 mmHg}}; the earliest sign is {{c2::pain on passive stretch}}.

cards.front: Weber C ankle fracture — level and significance?
cards.back: Fibular fracture above the syndesmosis → syndesmosis disrupted → unstable, usually needs ORIF ± syndesmotic screw.

head: Seddon
Sunderland

Recovery
rows: Myelin only (conduction block); no Wallerian degeneration

points: **Erb palsy**: upper trunk C5–C6 (Erb's point), excessive neck-shoulder separation; loss of shoulder abduction/external rotation and elbow flexion/supination; biceps reflex absent; 'waiter's tip'.

**Klumpke palsy**: lower trunk C8–T1, hyperabduction (grabbing a branch, breech delivery); claw hand of all fingers (intrinsics) ± **Horner syndrome** (T1 sympathetic) → pre-ganglionic, poor prognosis.
**Carpal tunnel syndrome**: Phalen (wrist flexion ~60 s), Tinel (tapping), Durkan compression test; NCS confirms; night splint/steroid injection → surgical release of flexor retinaculum.
**Froment sign**: pinching paper → thumb IP flexes (FPL, median) to compensate for weak adductor pollicis (ulnar).
**Ulnar paradox**: proximal (elbow) lesion gives LESS clawing than distal (wrist) because FDP to ring & little is also paralysed.
**Winging**: serratus anterior/long thoracic → medial winging; trapezius/spinal accessory → lateral winging.
Rate of regeneration ≈ 1 mm/day (≈1 inch/month); an advancing Tinel sign indicates regeneration.
Common peroneal is the most commonly injured nerve in the lower limb (winds around fibular neck); tibialis posterior (tibial nerve) keeps inversion intact.

traps.stem: Patient can extend the wrist (with radial deviation) but cannot extend the fingers at MCP; no sensory loss.
traps.trap: Radial nerve injury at spiral groove.
traps.fix: Posterior interosseous nerve palsy — ECRL (supplied above the split) is preserved and there is no sensory deficit.

traps.stem: Ulnar nerve lesion at the elbow shows milder clawing than one at the wrist.
traps.trap: So the elbow lesion must be partial.
traps.fix: Ulnar paradox: high lesion also paralyses ulnar half of FDP, so there is less DIP/PIP flexion and less clawing.

traps.stem: Brachial plexus injury in a newborn with ptosis and miosis on the same side.
traps.fix: Klumpke (C8–T1) with Horner — T1 root avulsion near the sympathetic chain; poor prognosis.

cards.text: Card test checks the {{c1::palmar interossei}} (adduction) and Froment sign checks the {{c2::adductor pollicis}} — both supplied by the {{c3::ulnar}} nerve.

cards.front: Fracture of the shaft humerus at the spiral groove: which nerve and which muscle is classically spared?
cards.back: Radial nerve; triceps spared (branches arise proximal to the groove) → wrist drop with intact elbow extension.

cards.front: Foot drop after fracture of the fibular neck — which movement is preserved and why?
cards.back: Inversion (tibialis posterior, tibial nerve). Common peroneal nerve loses dorsiflexion and eversion.

cards.front: Medial winging of the scapula after axillary clearance?
cards.back: Long thoracic nerve injury → serratus anterior paralysis.

title: Paediatric hip & foot, metabolic bone disease, TB spine, osteomyelitis
subject: Orthopedics
anchor: First-born breech girl, asymmetric thigh folds, Ortolani clunk → DDH → USG → Pavlik harness.
Boy 4–8 y, painless limp, ↓abduction & internal rotation → Perthes; obese 10–16 y boy with knee pain and obligatory external rotation on hip flexion → SCFE.
Back pain, gibbus, cold psoas abscess, paradiscal destruction → Pott's spine.
algorithm:
DDH by age
→ Newborn: Barlow (dislocatable: adduct + push posteriorly), Ortolani (reduces dislocated hip with abduction — clunk)
→ <4–6 months: ultrasound (Graf; α angle ≥60° normal) → Pavlik harness
→ 6–18 months: closed reduction (± adductor tenotomy) + hip spica
→ >18 months: open reduction ± pelvic/femoral osteotomy
→ X-ray after femoral head ossifies: Hilgenreiner & Perkin lines, broken Shenton line, ↑ acetabular index
SCFE
→ AP + frog-leg lateral (lateral more sensitive); Trethowan/Klein line fails to cut the epiphysis
→ Stable slip → in situ single cannulated screw fixation (no forcible reduction — AVN)
→ Unstable (cannot bear weight) → urgent fixation; consider prophylactic fixation of other hip in high-risk (endocrine, <10 y)

points: **CTEV** components: Cavus, forefoot Adductus, hindfoot Varus, Equinus — Ponseti corrects in **CAVE** order; cavus first by supinating forefoot (elevating first metatarsal), equinus last (percutaneous tendo-Achilles tenotomy in most); then foot abduction brace 23 h/day ~3 months then nights till ~4 y.
Primary deformity in CTEV is at the **talar neck** (medially and plantarly deviated); severity: Pirani score.
**Osteoporosis (DEXA)**: T-score ≤ −2.5 osteoporosis; −1 to −2.5 osteopenia; ≤ −2.5 + fragility fracture = severe; Z-score for children, premenopausal women, men <50; Ca, PO₄, ALP normal.
Osteoporosis drugs: bisphosphonates first-line; denosumab; teriparatide (anabolic, limited to ~2 y; osteosarcoma in rats).
**TB spine**: commonest skeletal TB; lower thoracic/thoracolumbar; paradiscal type commonest; MRI investigation of choice; cold abscess tracks (psoas → groin); ATT is mainstay ('middle path').
**Pott's paraplegia**: early onset (active disease, oedema/abscess/granulation — better prognosis) vs late onset (healed disease, >2 y; fibrosis/bony ridge/internal gibbus — poor prognosis).

**Acute osteomyelitis**: metaphysis of long bones in children (sluggish flow in hairpin vessels); S. aureus commonest; sickle cell disease classically Salmonella; MRI earliest; X-ray changes after ~10–14 days.
**Sequestrum** = dead bone; **involucrum** = new periosteal bone; **cloaca** = opening in involucrum; **Brodie abscess** = subacute localized metaphyseal abscess with sclerotic rim (proximal tibia).
Non-healing sinus of chronic osteomyelitis can develop squamous cell carcinoma (Marjolin ulcer).

traps.stem: 3-month-old girl with DDH; best initial imaging?
traps.fix: Ultrasound: femoral head is cartilaginous until ~4–6 months; X-ray becomes useful after ossification.

traps.stem: Obese 13-year-old boy complains only of knee pain; knee examination normal.
traps.fix: Examine & X-ray the hip (frog-leg lateral) — SCFE refers pain to knee via obturator nerve.

traps.stem: Child with sickle cell disease and osteomyelitis — characteristic organism?
traps.trap: Staph aureus is always the answer.
traps.fix: Salmonella is the classic exam association in sickle cell disease (S. aureus still common overall).

cards.text: Ponseti corrects CTEV in the order {{c1::C-A-V-E (cavus, adductus, varus, equinus)}}; equinus is usually corrected by {{c2::percutaneous tendo-Achilles tenotomy}}.

cards.front: Ortolani vs Barlow test?
cards.back: Ortolani: abduction reduces a dislocated hip (clunk). Barlow: adduction + posterior pressure dislocates a dislocatable hip.

cards.text: In SCFE, {{c1::Trethowan (Klein)}} line drawn along the superior femoral neck fails to intersect the epiphysis; treatment is {{c2::in situ screw fixation}}.

cards.front: White line of Frankel and Wimberger ring are features of?
cards.back: Scurvy (vitamin C deficiency).

title: Psychopharmacology: antipsychotics, clozapine, lithium, NMS vs serotonin syndrome
subject: Psychiatry
anchor: Fever + lead-pipe rigidity + ↑CK + altered sensorium days after haloperidol → NMS; hyperreflexia + clonus + diarrhoea + mydriasis within hours of adding a serotonergic drug → serotonin syndrome.
Lithium patient on a thiazide/NSAID with coarse tremor, ataxia, vomiting, confusion → lithium toxicity.
Treatment-resistant schizophrenia (failed 2 antipsychotics) → clozapine with ANC monitoring.

Clozapine initiation
→ Indication: treatment-resistant schizophrenia (≥2 adequate antipsychotic trials) or persistent suicidality in schizophrenia
→ Baseline ANC ≥1500/µL (≥1000 in benign ethnic neutropenia), ECG, weight, glucose, lipids
→ ANC weekly × 6 months → fortnightly months 6–12 → monthly thereafter
  ANC 1000–1499 (mild) → continue, monitor 3×/week

points: **Metabolic risk hierarchy**: clozapine ≈ olanzapine > quetiapine ≈ risperidone/paliperidone > ziprasidone ≈ aripiprazole ≈ lurasidone (lowest).

**Clozapine** adverse effects: agranulocytosis (~1%, mostly first 18 weeks), myocarditis (first 1–2 months), dose-related seizures, sialorrhoea (hypersalivation), constipation/ileus, weight gain, orthostasis; least EPS and lowest TD risk.
**Lithium**: therapeutic 0.6–1.2 mEq/L; toxicity >1.5; fine tremor at therapeutic level (propranolol) → coarse tremor in toxicity.

Lithium long-term: hypothyroidism (commonest endocrine), nephrogenic DI (polyuria — treat with amiloride), hyperparathyroidism/hypercalcaemia, weight gain, acne, psoriasis flare, leucocytosis, T-wave flattening, sinus node dysfunction.
Lithium in pregnancy: **Ebstein anomaly** (absolute risk small); levels ↑ by thiazides, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, dehydration, low-salt diet.

**Valproate**: neural tube defects (highest among AEDs), fetal valproate syndrome, ↓IQ/autism → avoid in women of child-bearing potential; also hepatotoxicity (<2 y), pancreatitis, PCOS, alopecia, thrombocytopenia.

**Carbamazepine**: NTD, craniofacial defects; SJS/TEN with HLA-B*15:02 (Asians); agranulocytosis/aplastic anaemia; hyponatraemia (SIADH); enzyme inducer (OCP failure). Lamotrigine: SJS (slow titration), relatively safer in pregnancy.

**SSRIs**: commonest early ADR GI upset; sexual dysfunction (commonest reason for stopping); hyponatraemia (elderly); bleeding with NSAIDs; QT (citalopram); suicidality warning <25 y; discontinuation syndrome worst with paroxetine, least with fluoxetine (long half-life); paroxetine – cardiac defects in pregnancy; sertraline preferred post-MI.
Hyperprolactinaemia worst with risperidone/paliperidone and typicals; aripiprazole lowers prolactin (partial agonist).

traps.stem: Patient on lithium is started on hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension and develops coarse tremor and ataxia.
traps.fix: Lithium toxicity — thiazides reduce lithium clearance (↑ proximal reabsorption); check level, stop drug.

traps.stem: Restless patient pacing the ward 1 week after starting haloperidol; nurse requests more haloperidol for 'agitation'.
traps.trap: Increase antipsychotic dose for worsening psychosis.
traps.fix: Akathisia — reduce dose, add propranolol/benzodiazepine; increasing the dose worsens it.

traps.stem: Tardive dyskinesia in a patient on long-term haloperidol — add trihexyphenidyl?
traps.fix: Anticholinergics worsen TD; reduce/stop the drug, switch to clozapine, use a VMAT2 inhibitor.

cards.text: Lithium therapeutic range {{c1::0.6–1.2 mEq/L}} (12 h post-dose); in pregnancy it is linked to {{c2::Ebstein anomaly}}; polyuria from {{c3::nephrogenic diabetes insipidus}} is treated with amiloride.

cards.front: NMS vs serotonin syndrome — the single best bedside discriminator?
cards.back: Reflexes/tone: NMS has lead-pipe rigidity with bradyreflexia; serotonin syndrome has hyperreflexia with clonus (and onset in hours).

cards.text: Clozapine is stopped when ANC falls below {{c1::500/µL}} (severe neutropenia); its most dangerous early cardiac complication is {{c2::myocarditis}}.

cards.front: Order of appearance of antipsychotic EPS?
cards.back: Acute dystonia (hours–days) → akathisia (days–weeks) → parkinsonism (weeks) → tardive dyskinesia (months–years).

cards.front: Antipsychotics with the highest and lowest metabolic risk?
cards.back: Highest: clozapine, olanzapine. Lowest: aripiprazole, ziprasidone, lurasidone.

cards.text: SSRI with the worst discontinuation syndrome is {{c1::paroxetine}}; least is {{c2::fluoxetine}} because of its long-acting metabolite norfluoxetine.

title: Schizophrenia spectrum, mood disorders, ECT & defence mechanisms
subject: Psychiatry
anchor: Voices commenting on actions, thought insertion/withdrawal/broadcast, delusional perception → Schneider first-rank symptoms (schizophrenia).
Duration decides the label: <1 month brief psychotic, 1–6 months schizophreniform, ≥6 months schizophrenia (DSM-5).
Mania ≥7 days (or hospitalised) → bipolar I; hypomania ≥4 days + major depression → bipolar II.

Mood episode concurrent with psychosis + ≥2 weeks of psychosis without mood symptoms
≥1 month of delusions; functioning relatively preserved; no prominent hallucinations
≥7 days (any duration if hospitalised); ≥3 symptoms (4 if mood only irritable)
≥4 days; no marked impairment, no psychosis, no hospitalisation

points: **Schneider FRS**: audible thoughts (thought echo), voices arguing/discussing, voices commenting, somatic passivity, thought withdrawal, insertion, broadcasting, made feelings, made impulses, made volitional acts, delusional perception — suggestive, not pathognomonic.
**Delusional perception** = normal perception followed by a delusional interpretation (two-stage); delusional mood (Wahnstimmung) often precedes it.
**Bleuler's 4 As**: autism, ambivalence, loosening of associations, affect (blunted).
Good prognosis schizophrenia: acute onset, late onset, clear precipitant, mood symptoms, positive symptoms, female, married, good premorbid function, family history of mood disorder.

**Delusional disorder types**: persecutory (commonest), jealous (Othello), erotomanic (de Clérambault), grandiose, somatic (incl. delusional parasitosis/Ekbom), mixed. Capgras = familiar person replaced by impostor; Fregoli = strangers are a familiar person in disguise; Cotard = nihilistic (psychotic depression, elderly).
**Bipolar I** needs only one manic episode; **bipolar II** never mania; rapid cycling = ≥4 episodes/year. Lithium is the mood stabiliser that reduces suicide.

**ECT indications**: severe depression with suicidality, psychotic depression, depressive stupor/food refusal, **catatonia** (best response; lorazepam first), refractory mania, NMS, treatment resistance; safe in pregnancy.

ECT has no absolute contraindication; raised intracranial pressure/space-occupying lesion is the most important relative one; also recent MI/stroke, aneurysm. Commonest side effect: transient memory impairment (retrograde > anterograde) and headache; bilateral more effective but more cognitive effects than right unilateral.
DSM-5 removed the bereavement exclusion for MDD; prolonged grief disorder added (DSM-5-TR).

traps.stem: Psychotic symptoms with FRS for 3 months, no mood episode.
traps.fix: Schizophreniform disorder (DSM-5: 1–6 months). Note: ICD-11 would call it schizophrenia (≥1 month).

traps.stem: Patient with recurrent major depression and a 5-day episode of elevated mood without impairment.
traps.fix: Bipolar II — hypomania (≥4 days, no marked impairment/psychosis) + major depression; any true mania = bipolar I.

traps.stem: Catatonic patient refusing food and fluids — first-line treatment?
traps.fix: Lorazepam challenge; ECT if no response. Antipsychotics can precipitate NMS in catatonia.

cards.text: DSM-5: brief psychotic disorder lasts {{c1::<1 month}}, schizophreniform {{c2::1–6 months}}, schizophrenia {{c3::≥6 months}}.

cards.front: Delusion that a spouse has been replaced by an identical impostor?
cards.back: Capgras syndrome (delusional misidentification).

cards.text: Hypomania requires ≥{{c1::4}} days; mania requires ≥{{c2::7}} days or hospitalisation.

cards.front: Best-responding indication for ECT?
cards.back: Catatonia (also psychotic/suicidal depression).

cards.front: Suppression vs repression?
cards.back: Suppression: conscious, mature defence. Repression: unconscious pushing away of unacceptable thoughts (neurotic).

cards.text: In {{c1::delusional perception}}, a normal perception is given a sudden delusional meaning — a Schneiderian first-rank symptom.

cards.front: Discriminator: NMS vs serotonin syndrome — deciding feature?
cards.back: NMS: slow onset (days), lead-pipe rigidity, bradyreflexia, ↑CPK, dopamine blocker. Serotonin syndrome: rapid onset (<24 h), clonus + hyperreflexia, diarrhoea, mydriasis, serotonergic drug.

cards.front: Discriminator: Schizophrenia vs schizophreniform vs brief psychotic disorder — duration?
cards.back: Brief psychotic: <1 month; schizophreniform: 1–6 months; schizophrenia: ≥6 months (DSM-5).

verify: DSM-5-TR (2022) criteria; ICD-11 uses ≥1 month for schizophrenia. Kaplan & Sadock 12e.
algorithm:
Hyperthermia + altered sensorium + rigidity/tone — which syndrome? Look at ONSET, REFLEXES, PUPILS, BOWEL
→ Drug exposure timeline?
  Antipsychotic (dopamine blocker) days–weeks, slow onset (1–3 days) , lead-pipe rigidity, bradyreflexia, ↑CPK → Neuroleptic malignant syndrome → stop drug, cooling, bromocriptine / dantrolene
  Serotonergic drug (SSRI + MAOI, tramadol, linezolid, ondansetron) rapid onset (<24 h), hyperreflexia + clonus (esp. lower limbs), mydriasis, diarrhoea → Serotonin syndrome → stop drug, benzodiazepines, cyproheptadine

→ Discriminator in one line: NMS = rigid + slow + no clonus; Serotonin = clonus + fast + diarrhoea

title: Alcohol & opioids, anxiety/OCD/trauma, somatic, personality, child psychiatry, MHCA 2017
subject: Psychiatry
anchor: Day 3 after last drink: confusion, visual hallucinations, tremor, tachycardia, fever → delirium tremens → benzodiazepines.
Alcoholic with confusion, ophthalmoplegia/nystagmus, ataxia → Wernicke → IV thiamine BEFORE glucose.
Pinpoint pupils + respiratory depression + coma → opioid overdose → naloxone; dilated pupils, yawning, lacrimation, piloerection, diarrhoea → opioid withdrawal.
algorithm:
Alcohol withdrawal
→ Assess CIWA-Ar (10 items, max 67)
  <8–10 → supportive, monitor
  ≥10 → symptom-triggered benzodiazepine (chlordiazepoxide/diazepam)
  Liver disease / elderly → lorazepam or oxazepam (no active metabolites)
→ Thiamine for all (IV high dose if Wernicke suspected) before glucose; correct Mg, K
→ Seizure → benzodiazepine (phenytoin not useful)
→ After detox: relapse prevention — naltrexone, acamprosate (safe in liver disease), disulfiram (supervised, motivated, abstinent ≥12 h), baclofen
Opioid overdose → airway + naloxone IV/IM/IN, repeat (short half-life → re-sedation)
Opioid dependence → buprenorphine (± naloxone) or methadone maintenance; naltrexone after 7–10 days opioid-free

points: **Wernicke** (reversible): confusion, ophthalmoplegia (lateral rectus palsy, nystagmus), ataxia — full triad uncommon; mammillary bodies. **Korsakoff** (largely irreversible): anterograde > retrograde amnesia, confabulation; dorsomedial thalamus.
Most specific lab marker of chronic heavy drinking: carbohydrate-deficient transferrin; GGT and MCV raised; AST:ALT >2.
**OCD**: ego-dystonic obsessions + compulsions; contamination commonest; first-line SSRI (higher doses, longer trial) + ERP; clomipramine; antipsychotic augmentation; DBS for refractory.

**PTSD** symptoms >1 month (acute stress disorder: 3 days–1 month); intrusion, avoidance, negative cognition/mood, hyperarousal; trauma-focused CBT/EMDR + SSRI; prazosin for nightmares. **Adjustment disorder**: within 3 months of stressor.

**Panic disorder**: recurrent unexpected attacks peaking within minutes + ≥1 month worry; SSRI + CBT. **GAD** ≥6 months. Specific phobia → systematic desensitisation (Wolpe); performance anxiety → propranolol.

**Conversion (functional neurological) disorder**: unconscious, primary gain, la belle indifférence; **factitious**: intentional production for sick role (Munchausen; by proxy); **malingering**: intentional for external gain; **illness anxiety**: fear of having disease with minimal symptoms.

**Personality clusters**: A odd (paranoid, schizoid, schizotypal); B dramatic (antisocial, borderline, histrionic, narcissistic); C anxious (avoidant, dependent, obsessive-compulsive). Borderline → splitting, self-harm, DBT. Antisocial needs age ≥18 + conduct disorder before 15.

**ADHD**: symptoms before age 12, ≥6 months, ≥2 settings; methylphenidate first-line (≥6 y), atomoxetine non-stimulant. **Autism**: social-communication deficit + restricted repetitive behaviour from early childhood; M-CHAT screen 18–24 months; risperidone/aripiprazole for irritability only.

**MHCA 2017**: attempted suicide presumed due to severe stress (Sec 115) — effectively decriminalised; advance directives & nominated representative; ECT without anaesthesia and muscle relaxant prohibited; ECT banned for minors except with guardian consent + Mental Health Review Board permission; no chaining, no sterilisation as treatment; emergency treatment up to 72 h; supported admission up to 30 days (Sec 89).

traps.stem: Alcoholic with cirrhosis in withdrawal — benzodiazepine of choice?
traps.fix: Lorazepam/oxazepam: conjugated by glucuronidation, no active metabolites — safe in hepatic impairment (and elderly).

traps.stem: Malnourished alcoholic, hypoglycaemic and confused, in ED.
traps.fix: Give IV thiamine before/with glucose — glucose load can precipitate or worsen Wernicke encephalopathy.

traps.stem: Heroin user who used 2 h ago is given the first dose of buprenorphine and becomes acutely ill with withdrawal.
traps.fix: Precipitated withdrawal — high-affinity partial agonist displaces full agonist; start only once objective withdrawal is present (COWS).

cards.text: Alcohol withdrawal: tremor at {{c1::6–12 h}}, seizures at {{c2::12–48 h}}, delirium tremens at {{c3::48–96 h}}.

cards.front: Alcohol relapse-prevention drug safe in liver disease?
cards.back: Acamprosate (renally excreted, NMDA modulator); avoid in renal failure.

cards.text: Korsakoff syndrome: {{c1::anterograde}} amnesia with {{c2::confabulation}}, largely irreversible; Wernicke is reversible with {{c3::thiamine}}.

cards.front: Conversion disorder vs factitious disorder vs malingering?
cards.back: Conversion: unconscious symptom production (primary gain). Factitious: intentional, to assume sick role. Malingering: intentional, for external gain (money, avoiding duty).

cards.text: Under MHCA 2017, ECT may not be given without {{c1::anaesthesia and muscle relaxant}}, and attempted suicide is presumed to result from {{c2::severe stress}} (Section 115).

cards.front: Cluster C personality disorders?
cards.back: Avoidant, dependent, obsessive-compulsive (anxious/fearful cluster).

title: Papulosquamous disorders: psoriasis, lichen planus, pityriasis rosea, PRP, seborrhoeic dermatitis
subject: Dermatology
anchor: Well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scale on extensors/scalp, nail pitting, Auspitz sign → psoriasis.
Pruritic, purple, polygonal, planar papules on wrist flexors with Wickham striae and lacy buccal white lines → lichen planus.
Single oval herald patch followed in 1–2 weeks by a 'Christmas tree' truncal eruption in a young adult → pityriasis rosea.

points: **Grattage test**: scraping → candle-grease scale → Bulkley membrane → **Auspitz sign** (pinpoint bleeding from dilated papillary capillaries).
**Koebner (isomorphic) phenomenon**: psoriasis, lichen planus, vitiligo, (pseudo-Koebner in warts, molluscum).

**Psoriasis types**: plaque (commonest), guttate (children, after streptococcal throat infection), erythrodermic, pustular (von Zumbusch — after systemic steroid withdrawal; impetigo herpetiformis in pregnancy), inverse/flexural, palmoplantar; HLA-C*06:02 (Cw6).
**Nails**: pitting commonest; oil-drop (salmon patch) most specific; onycholysis, subungual hyperkeratosis. Psoriatic arthritis: DIP involvement, arthritis mutilans, pencil-in-cup.
**Drugs that worsen psoriasis**: lithium, β-blockers, antimalarials, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, interferon, abrupt systemic steroid withdrawal.
**PASI** scores erythema, induration, scaling (0–4) and area (0–6) for head, trunk, upper & lower limbs → 0–72; PASI 75 = 75% improvement (trial endpoint); 'rule of tens' for severe disease.

**Lichen planus**: 6 Ps (pruritic, purple, polygonal, planar, papules, plaques); oral reticular LP commonest oral form; nail pterygium; association with **hepatitis C**; erosive oral LP → SCC risk; lichenoid drugs: gold, antimalarials, β-blockers, thiazides.

**Pityriasis rosea**: herald patch with peripheral collarette scale; lesions along Langer's lines (Christmas tree on back); HHV-6/7 implicated; self-limited 6–8 weeks; always exclude secondary syphilis (VDRL) if palms/soles involved.

**PRP**: follicular 'nutmeg-grater' papules on dorsal proximal phalanges, salmon-orange erythroderma with islands of sparing, orange waxy palmoplantar keratoderma; histology checkerboard ortho-/parakeratosis; Griffiths type I (classic adult) commonest.
**Seborrhoeic dermatitis**: greasy yellow scales on scalp, eyebrows, nasolabial folds, presternum; Malassezia; cradle cap in infants; severe in HIV and Parkinson's disease; ketoconazole.

traps.stem: Lesion with Koebner phenomenon and thick scale; biopsy shows saw-tooth rete ridges and band-like lymphocytic infiltrate.
traps.fix: Lichen planus; Koebner occurs in both. Saw-tooth rete + hypergranulosis + band-like infiltrate = LP; psoriasis has regular acanthosis, parakeratosis and Munro microabscesses.

traps.stem: Psoriasis patient whose plaques turn into widespread sterile pustules with fever after oral prednisolone is stopped.
traps.fix: Generalised pustular (von Zumbusch) psoriasis triggered by systemic steroid withdrawal — avoid systemic steroids in psoriasis; acitretin/cyclosporine.

traps.stem: Herald-patch-like eruption on trunk with lesions on palms and soles.
traps.fix: Palm/sole involvement is atypical for PR — test for secondary syphilis (VDRL/TPHA).

cards.text: In psoriasis, neutrophils in the stratum corneum form {{c1::Munro microabscesses}}, and in the stratum spinosum form the {{c2::spongiform pustule of Kogoj}}.

cards.front: Histological correlate of Wickham striae?
cards.back: Focal wedge-shaped hypergranulosis (thickened granular layer) in lichen planus.

cards.text: Civatte (colloid) bodies are {{c1::apoptotic basal keratinocytes}} seen in {{c2::lichen planus}}.

cards.front: Most common and most specific nail findings in psoriasis?
cards.back: Commonest: pitting. Most specific: oil-drop (salmon) patch.

cards.text: Pityriasis rosea starts with a {{c1::herald patch}} and the secondary eruption follows {{c2::Langer's (cleavage) lines}} in a Christmas-tree pattern.

cards.front: Systemic drug of choice for generalised pustular psoriasis (non-pregnant) and the key counselling point?
cards.back: Acitretin — teratogenic; avoid pregnancy for 3 years after stopping.

points: **Nikolsky sign** positive: pemphigus vulgaris & foliaceus, SSSS, TEN; negative in BP, DH.
**Pemphigus antigen rule**: mucosal-dominant PV = anti-Dsg3 only; mucocutaneous PV = Dsg3 + Dsg1; PF = Dsg1 only (desmoglein compensation theory).
**Drug-induced pemphigus**: thiol drugs (penicillamine, captopril) — usually foliaceus pattern. **Drug-induced BP**: DPP-4 inhibitors (gliptins), furosemide, spironolactone.
**SSSS vs TEN**: SSSS — child, exfoliative toxin cleaves Dsg1 → subcorneal/granular split, mucosa spared, no drug; TEN — full-thickness epidermal necrosis, mucosa involved, drug-induced.

**SJS/TEN culprits**: allopurinol, carbamazepine (HLA-B*15:02), phenytoin, lamotrigine, phenobarbital, sulfonamides (cotrimoxazole), nevirapine, oxicam NSAIDs; typically 4–28 days after starting drug.
**DH**: almost all patients have gluten-sensitive enteropathy (mostly asymptomatic); dapsone relieves itch within days but not the gut; gluten-free diet reduces enteropathy-associated lymphoma risk.
**Mucous membrane (cicatricial) pemphigoid**: mucosal scarring, ocular symblepharon → blindness; **pemphigoid gestationis**: BP180, linear C3, periumbilical onset in pregnancy.
Tzanck smear: acantholytic cells (PV); multinucleated giant cells (herpes).

traps.stem: Elderly diabetic on sitagliptin with tense bullae, Nikolsky negative.
traps.trap: Pemphigus vulgaris — commonest blistering disease asked.
traps.fix: Bullous pemphigoid (gliptin-induced); tense subepidermal blisters with linear IgG/C3 at BMZ; stop the gliptin.

traps.stem: DIF shows granular IgA in dermal papillae; what is the target antigen?
traps.fix: Epidermal transglutaminase (TG3) is the cutaneous autoantigen; anti-tTG serology is still used for screening.

traps.stem: Feverish 3-year-old with tender erythema and superficial peeling, mouth spared; no drug history.
traps.fix: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome — subcorneal split (Dsg1 cleavage by exfoliative toxin), mucosa spared; antistaphylococcal antibiotics.

cards.back: BP180 (BPAG2, collagen XVII) and BP230 (BPAG1); linear IgG and C3 along the basement membrane zone.

cards.text: Dermatitis herpetiformis: {{c1::granular IgA}} at dermal papillae; rapid response to {{c2::dapsone}}; long-term control with {{c3::gluten-free diet}}.

cards.front: Pemphigus foliaceus vs vulgaris — mucosa and antigen?
cards.back: Foliaceus: Dsg1, subcorneal split, mucosa spared. Vulgaris: Dsg3 (± Dsg1), suprabasal split, mucosa involved.

cards.front: Discriminator: Pemphigus vulgaris vs bullous pemphigoid — deciding feature?
cards.back: Pemphigus: intraepidermal acantholysis, flaccid bullae, Nikolsky +, IgG to desmoglein 3 (net-like/'chicken-wire' IF), oral lesions. Pemphigoid: subepidermal split, tense bullae, Nikolsky −, anti-BP180/BP230, linear IF at BMZ, elderly.

cards.front: Discriminator: Dermatitis herpetiformis vs linear IgA disease — deciding feature?
cards.back: DH: granular IgA at dermal papillary tips, coeliac association. Linear IgA: linear IgA along BMZ, drug-induced (vancomycin).

points: **Ridley-Jopling**: TT – BT – BB – BL – LL (+ indeterminate). Lepromin (Mitsuda) test: strongly positive TT, negative LL — prognostic, not diagnostic.
**WHO classification**: PB = 1–5 skin lesions, no bacilli on smear; MB = ≥6 lesions, or nerve involvement, or smear-positive regardless of lesion count (NLEP: PB ≤1 nerve, MB >1 nerve).

**WHO MDT (2018)**: rifampicin + dapsone + clofazimine for both — PB 6 months, MB 12 months. Monthly supervised: rifampicin 600 mg + clofazimine 300 mg; daily: dapsone 100 mg + clofazimine 50 mg (adult). Older regimen: PB = rifampicin + dapsone only.

**Type 1 (reversal) reaction**: borderline cases, type IV hypersensitivity, existing lesions inflame + neuritis → oral prednisolone. **Type 2 (ENL)**: BL/LL, immune-complex (type III), crops of tender evanescent nodules with fever, neuritis, iritis, orchitis → prednisolone; thalidomide for recurrent ENL; continue MDT during reactions.

LL features: leonine facies, madarosis (lateral eyebrow first), saddle nose, glove-and-stocking anaesthesia, globi/lepra (Virchow) cells, Grenz zone; Fite-Faraco stain; M. leprae not cultivable (mouse footpad, armadillo).

**Dermatophytes**: Trichophyton (skin, hair, nail), Microsporum (skin, hair — not nail), Epidermophyton (skin, nail — not hair). Tinea capitis needs oral therapy (griseofulvin for Microsporum, terbinafine for Trichophyton).

**Wood's lamp**: Microsporum tinea capitis — bright green; favus (T. schoenleinii) — dull green; T. tonsurans (endothrix) — none; pityriasis versicolor — yellow/golden; erythrasma — coral red; Pseudomonas — green; vitiligo — chalky white; porphyria (urine) — pink-red.

**Scabies**: burrow pathognomonic; finger webs, wrists, axillae, nipples, umbilicus, genitalia (nodules), face spared in adults but not infants; permethrin 5% neck-down, repeat at 1 week, treat all contacts; oral ivermectin 200 µg/kg × 2 doses (not <15 kg/pregnancy); crusted (Norwegian) scabies in immunocompromised — huge mite load.

**Syphilis serology**: non-treponemal (VDRL/RPR) — screening, titre for activity & response (4-fold fall), become negative after cure, biological false positives (pregnancy, SLE/APLA, leprosy, malaria, HIV), prozone in secondary syphilis; treponemal (TPHA, FTA-ABS) — confirmatory, stay positive for life; FTA-ABS earliest serology to turn positive.
**Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction**: fever, myalgia within 24 h of first penicillin dose (commonest in secondary syphilis) — not allergy, continue treatment.

traps.stem: Painful genital ulcer with a single fluctuant unilateral inguinal bubo; Gram stain shows chains of Gram-negative rods.
traps.fix: Chancroid: painful ulcer + suppurative unilateral bubo + 'school of fish'; LGV's primary ulcer is painless and transient and buboes show the groove sign.

traps.stem: Secondary syphilis with florid rash but VDRL non-reactive on undiluted serum.
traps.fix: Prozone phenomenon — antibody excess; repeat VDRL on diluted serum.

traps.stem: Leprosy patient on MDT develops new painful red nodules with fever and orchitis.
traps.fix: Type 2 reaction (ENL); continue MDT, give prednisolone (thalidomide for recurrent ENL).

cards.back: Type 1 (reversal): delayed (type IV) hypersensitivity in borderline leprosy. Type 2 (ENL): immune-complex (type III) in BL/LL.

subject: Dermatology
anchor: Changing mole: Asymmetry, Border irregular, Colour variegated, Diameter >6 mm, Evolving → melanoma → excision biopsy; Breslow thickness drives prognosis.
Elderly, central face, pearly rolled edge with telangiectasia, slowly eroding → BCC (rodent ulcer); ulcer with everted edge in a burn scar → SCC (Marjolin).
Velvety hyperpigmented neck/axillae in obese → insulin resistance; sudden widespread with tripe palms in elderly → gastric adenocarcinoma.

points: **Breslow thickness** (granular layer to deepest tumour cell, mm) = most important prognostic factor of a localised primary melanoma; sentinel-node status is the strongest overall predictor. AJCC 8: T1 ≤1.0 mm (T1a <0.8 mm, no ulceration), T2 >1–2, T3 >2–4, T4 >4 mm; ulceration adds 'b'. **Clark level** (I epidermis → V subcutis) is anatomical and no longer used in AJCC 8.

Melanoma margins: in situ 0.5–1 cm; ≤1 mm → 1 cm; 1–2 mm → 1–2 cm; >2 mm → 2 cm. Markers S-100, HMB-45, Melan-A, SOX10; BRAF V600E (~50%) → BRAF + MEK inhibitors; immunotherapy (anti-PD-1, anti-CTLA-4).

**Fitzpatrick skin types**: I always burns, never tans · II usually burns, tans minimally · III sometimes burns, tans gradually · IV rarely burns, tans well · V very rarely burns, brown skin · VI never burns, deeply pigmented. Most Indians are types IV–V.

**Vitiligo**: autoimmune loss of melanocytes; Koebner +; leukotrichia = poor prognosis for repigmentation; segmental (early onset, stable, poor medical response → grafting) vs non-segmental (commonest); stable ≥1 year before surgery; treatment topical steroid/tacrolimus, NB-UVB, oral mini-pulse dexamethasone for spreading disease, topical ruxolitinib; associations thyroid disease, diabetes, pernicious anaemia, alopecia areata.

**Melasma**: symmetric facial hyperpigmentation (centrofacial commonest) in women; pregnancy (chloasma), OCPs, UV; Wood's lamp accentuates epidermal type; strict sunscreen + triple combination (hydroquinone + tretinoin + fluocinolone) ± oral tranexamic acid; hydroquinone overuse → exogenous ochronosis.

**Acne (Indian grading)**: Grade 1 comedones ± occasional papules · Grade 2 papules, comedones, few pustules · Grade 3 predominant pustules, nodules, abscesses · Grade 4 cysts, abscesses, sinuses (acne conglobata). **Isotretinoin** for nodulocystic/scarring/refractory acne: teratogenic (pregnancy test, contraception, avoid pregnancy 1 month after stopping), cheilitis commonest, ↑TG/LFTs; never with tetracyclines (pseudotumour cerebri); no blood donation.

**Alopecia**: areata — patchy smooth, exclamation-mark hairs, nail pitting, ophiasis = poor prognosis, intralesional triamcinolone/JAK inhibitors; androgenetic — miniaturisation, Hamilton-Norwood/Ludwig, minoxidil ± finasteride; telogen effluvium — diffuse shedding 2–3 months after a stressor, self-limiting; anagen effluvium — chemotherapy within weeks; scarring — DLE, lichen planopilaris, pseudopelade ('footprints in snow').

**Nails**: pitting (psoriasis, alopecia areata), pterygium (LP), koilonychia (iron deficiency), Beau lines (systemic illness), Mees lines (arsenic), Muehrcke lines (hypoalbuminaemia, blanch on pressure), Terry nails (cirrhosis), half-and-half/Lindsay (CKD), splinter haemorrhage (endocarditis), blue lunula (Wilson, argyria), periungual fibroma/Koenen tumour (tuberous sclerosis).

**Cutaneous markers**: necrobiosis lipoidica (diabetes; yellow-brown atrophic shin plaques with telangiectasia), diabetic dermopathy (commonest diabetic skin sign), erythema nodosum (septal panniculitis without vasculitis — streptococcal infection, TB, sarcoidosis/Löfgren, IBD, OCP, pregnancy), pyoderma gangrenosum (IBD, RA, myeloma; pathergy), Sweet syndrome (AML), necrolytic migratory erythema (glucagonoma), Leser-Trélat (sudden seborrhoeic keratoses — GI adenocarcinoma), Bazex (aerodigestive SCC), Gottron papules/heliotrope (dermatomyositis).

traps.stem: Pigmented lesion on the sole of an Indian man with pigment extending onto the proximal nail fold.
traps.trap: Superficial spreading melanoma — commonest type overall.
traps.fix: Acral lentiginous melanoma — commonest melanoma in dark-skinned populations; periungual pigment = Hutchinson's sign.

traps.stem: Which single feature best predicts outcome of a clinically localised primary melanoma?
traps.fix: Breslow thickness (with ulceration); Clark level is dropped from AJCC 8 staging.

traps.stem: Acne patient on doxycycline is started on isotretinoin and develops headache with papilloedema.
traps.trap: Migraine from drug side effect — continue both.
traps.fix: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension — isotretinoin + tetracyclines are contraindicated together; stop them.

cards.text: Breslow thickness is measured from the {{c1::granular layer}} to the {{c2::deepest tumour cell}}; AJCC 8 T1a is <{{c3::0.8}} mm without ulceration.

cards.front: Commonest melanoma subtype overall vs in Indians?
cards.back: Overall: superficial spreading. Indians/dark skin: acral lentiginous.

cards.text: BCC histology shows {{c1::peripheral palisading}} with retraction artefact; it is linked to {{c2::PTCH1}} mutation (Gorlin syndrome).

cards.front: Exclamation-mark hairs indicate?
cards.back: Alopecia areata (hairs tapering towards the scalp).

cards.text: Necrobiosis lipoidica is associated with {{c1::diabetes mellitus}}; erythema nodosum is a {{c2::septal}} panniculitis without vasculitis.

cards.front: Fitzpatrick type IV vs V?
cards.back: IV: rarely burns, tans well (moderate brown). V: very rarely burns, dark brown skin.
